summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 (the respective valuation dates being March 31, 1965, March 31. The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 estimated as the accrued interest on the assessee 's money lending investments. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and urged that as it maintained its books of account in accordance with the cash system of accounting the accrued interests on the money lending investment could not be included in the wealth tax assessments. The Appellate Tribunal held favour with the Appellate Tribunal. In doing so, the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner followed "Commissioner of Wealth Tax Bihar and Orissa vs Vysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju (Orissa)(1), The Wealth tax Officer appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. Under section 3 of the Wealth Tax Act, wealth tax is charged for every assessment year in respect of the net wealth of the assessee on the corresponding valuation date. The expression "net wealth" is defined by cl. (m) of s.2 of the Act as "the amount by which the aggregate value . Of all the assets, wherever located, belonging to the assessee, on the valuation date". [310C] 2.1 In the instant case, the assets are not confined to cash. Where the asset is an asset other than cash, its value is determined pursuant to sub section (I) of section 7 as the estimated price, which, in the opinion of the Income Tax Officer, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the valu date. In other words, it would be the estimated open market value of the rights in the property which constitute the asset.

Respondent in the appeal was a Time Keeper in Beas Sutlej Link Project, Sundernagar. He was incharge of preparing the pay bills and other bills of the work charg ed employees of the project. He made this entry with ulterior motive to withdraw the pay of Ashok Kumar for the month of May 1969 even though Ash ok Kumar was not working in that Division. A bogus identi ty card in the name of Ashok kumar T.No. 59 T with the sign a tures of the issuing officer was also prepared by the r e spondent although it was not his duty to prepare the ident i ty card. The said fictitious identity card was used by o ne Suraj Singh, cleaner T. No. 210 K of Beggi Tunnelling Divi sion for the purpose of withdrawing the pay. While Suraj Singh by impersonation was receiving the pay ment of Ashok Kuma r, he was recognised by the Cashier since he kn ew him personally. There then started an enquiry followed by departmental proceedings against three persons includ ing the respondent herein. The Personnel Officer of the 23 BSL Project was appointed as Inquiry Officer. He framed charge against the responde nt in the following terms: "That the said Shri Parma Nand, while working as Time Keeper, in time Keeping Sub Division of Beasput Li nk Project, Sundarnagar during the month May 1969 failed to maintain absolute integrity and devotion to duty in as mu ch he falsely marked the attendance of Shri Ashok Kumar Token N o. 59 at serial No. 10 on page 2 of the relevant pay roll. " The Inquiry Officer framed charges against the respondent in the above terms: That the said Sri Parma n Nand, While working as time Keeper in Time Keeping Sub division of Sundernagar during th month of June 1969 failed t hat he failed to maintaining absolute integrity & devotion to duties in as much as he falsely mark ed the attendance. An appreciation of the evidence, as done in the preceding pages, would sh ow that the applicant had entered the name o f Ashok Kumar in the pay roll for May 1969 and so far as other other eviden ce against him is concerned, it is mostly of a circumstanti al nature. There was no direct or expert evidence that it was he who had initiated t he identity card. It was ly contended on behalf of the appel lant that if the enquiry held against the delinquent offi cer was proper with the findings supported by evidence, the Tribunal cannot substitute its own judgment to mod i fy the punishment awarded. On the other hand, an order bas ed on several grounds some of which are found to be non existent or irrelevant, and there is nothing to show that the authori ty would have passed the order on t he basis of the other relevant and existing grounds, and t he exclusion of the irrelevant or non exist ent grounds cou ld not have affected the ultimate opinion or decision. In dismissing th at appeal, Shalat, J., made inter alia, the following observ a tions: "The findings in respect of charges l(a) and l(e) 29 should be set aside as being opposed to the rules of natur al justice, but the findings in regard of charge l(c) a nd l(d) need not be disturbed. It will be left to Government to decide whether, on the basis of t he charges, the punishment of dismissal should be maintain ed or else whether a lesser punishment would suffice." The Supreme Court reversed this order on the ground that it is not commensurate with t he delinquency of the official. The constitutional guarantee afforded to a publ ic servant is that he shall not be dismissed or removed by an authority subordinate to that by which he was appointed, a nd that he shah not be dismiss ed or reduced in ra nk until he has been given a reasonable opportunity of showi ng against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him.

The appellants are the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff in a suit for declaration and an injunction to restrain the defendants from dispossessing him from the property known as 'Palmar Oiteral do Predio Aivao ' comprising seven lots of coconut grove situated at Caranzalem belonging to defendant No. 2. The said suit was dismissed on Match 28, 1974 on the ground that the plaintiff was no more in possession of the suit property and, therefore, a suit was for a mere declaration simpliciter could not lie. On the dismissal of the said suit, the original plaintiff filed another suit No. 114/74 on May 6, 1974 for restoration of possession on the grounds that he was the lawful tenant of the property and since he had not been dispossessed, in accordance with law, the defen dants who were mere trespassers were liable to be evicted therefrom. The Trial Court upheld the plaintiffs contention that the suit was barred by res judicata as well as Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High Court dismissed the suit holding that the subject matter of the second suit was directly and substantially in issue in the previous suit between the same parties and hence regardless of the relief claimed, the second Suit was clearly barred by Order 2 rule 2(2)(3)of the Code. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the Civil Court is specifically barred by sub section (2) of Section 58 from settling, deciding or dealing with any question which is required to be settled, decided and dealt with by the Mamlatdar. There can, therefore be no doubt that after the Fifth Amendment became effective in regard to land used primarily for growing coconut trees and garden produce, the jurisdiction of Civil Court was ousted by virtue of section 58(2) from settling decide, deciding and dealing with such question as : (i) Whether any person is a tenant or should be deemed to be a tenant under the Act, the Mamlatdar shall decide such question; (ii) Whether the tenancy of any deemed tenant is legally terminated and if no, whether the tenant evicted from the land held by him as such is entitled to restoration of Possession? The jurisdiction is, therefore vested in the Mamlatdar under Section 7 read with section 58 of the Act and section 58 (2), specifically bars the jurisdictionof all other courts to settle, decide or deal with any questions which is by or under the act required to he settled, decide, decided or dealt with; (iii) Whether a person is not a tenant in respect of the lands in question should be referred to the Mamlatdar for decision and after his decision is received by the Civil court if the issue is held against defendant No1, the Civil Judge may consider passing of a decree in eviction but if on the other hand he is held to be tenant, the civil Court may be required to dismiss the suit.

The petitioners are carpenters 1st and 2 grade employed at the Wood Working Centre of the Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation (the Corpo ration). They are termed as daily rated employees. In this petition under Article 32 of the Constitution, they are seeking enforcement of their fundamental right to have "equal pay for equal work". They demand payment in terms paid to their counterparts in regular services. They want the same pay of the regular employees as carpenter or in the alternative, the minimum wages prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner for like categories of workmen. They also seek regularisation of their services with the benefits of pen sion, gratuity etc. The Corporation resisted the petitioners ' claim and contended that the unit where the petition ers are working is a factory registered under the Factories Act, and as such, the question of payment to the petitioners does not arise. A little more information about the purpose and object of the Corpora tion would be useful for proper understanding of the case. The Corpora tation has been kept alive. But to avoid or minimise further loss, it is stated that the Corporation has reduced its overheads and maintained only the administrative staff in the production centers at different parts of the State and no permanent craftsmen are employed. With these facts, the Court directed the Central Government to fix the pay scale of the petitioners on par with his counterparts doing identical work under the same employer. In the immediate aftermath of the decision in Randhir Singh vs Union of India, ; this Court in Randhir singh vs Union Of India, , has innovated that it is a constitu tional goal capable of being achieved through constitutional remedies. There the Court pointed out that principle has to be read into Article 14 of the Constitu tion which enjoins the State not to deny any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the law and also to Article 16 which declares that there should be equality of opportu nity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State. The principle of "equal Pay for equal Work" has no mechanical application in every case of similar work. Article 14 permits reasonable classification rounded on rational basis. It is, therefore not impermissible to provide two different pay scales in the same cadre on the basis of selection based on merit with due regard to experience and seniority. It was pointed out by this Court that in service, merit or experience could be the proper basis for classification to promote efficiency in administration and he or sheearns also by experience as much as by other means. Apart from that, the court has expressly observed that the higher pay scale to avoid stagnation or resultant frustration for lack of promotional avenues may also be allowed. Meva Ram Kanojia vs All India Institute of Medical Sciences and Anr., ; , referred to.

The prosecution alleged that in pursuance of the conspiracy and in furtherance of their common intention they committed murder of one Malan on or about 29.11.1975, while accused 1 and 6 were tried for three murders of two young girls and a women alleged to have been committed them and the approver P.W. 1 committed three murders. The Sessions Judge found that the evidence against accused 1 to 4 was not guilty of the charge of conspiracy framed under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and acquitted accused 7 and convicted accused 1 alone. Accused 5 and 6 filed Criminal Appeal No. 288 of 1980 respectively against their conviction and sentence awarded to them. The High Court allowed the appeal of accused 1, and set aside his conviction and the sentence awarded by the trial court under section302 read with Section 34 I P.C. and acquitted him. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the charge under section 120B I. P. C. was framed against four named persons who had been arrayed as accused 1 in respect of the murder of Malan, and that in view of the acquittal of all the seven accused by the Trial Court of charge No. 1 framed under Section 302 readwith Section 34 IPC, no appeal against their acquittal had been filed in the High Court and also the fact that accused 5 was not a party to charge No 4 which was framed only against accused 2,3,4 and 7. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.

The appellant 's property was sought to be sold by the respondent I on August 22, 1945. The recitals in the will clearly and specifically stated that the testatrix had the knowledge of the contents of the Will; that after her death the document would remain with the appellant and it added that the plaintiff had not executed any prior will but that in case any such will has been executed by her the same stood cancelled by the execution of the present will; and on the evidence, the sound and disposing state of mind. The High Court held that even if it had found in favour of the appellant on these two points it would not have been of any help to him because his case must inevitably fail when it is held that the will set up by him was not proved to be the last will and testament of Lakshmamma. Held, further, that after the fact that the testator was ill at Mandya and had received substantial benefit under the will and since the appellant had taken a leading part in its execution, the onus was heavy on him to remove the suspicions attending execution of a document and to establish that the executant fully understood the nature of the recitals in his preamble and the effect of the dispositions before she put her signature to the document of his own free will. The fact that after his death the testatrix has not executed anything more than an act of undue influence can not exonerate him of any possible doubt. There may be other suspicious circumstances attending on the execution. It may, however, be stated generally that a propounder of the will has to prove the due and valid execution of his will and that if there are any suspicious circumstances surrounding the execution must remove those doubts from the mind of the court by cogent and satisfactory evidence. The propounder would be called upon to show by satisfactory evidence that the document so propounded is the last Will of a free and capable testator 's signature on it when she was in a sound disposing state or of mind as required by law, courts would be justified in making a finding in favour Of the propounder.

The appellant company manufactured Arcons, known as "Cinema Arc Carbons", manufactured by the appellant company. The Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal allowed an application for adducing expert evidence to determine the question whether are carbons manufactured by it could be covered by the entry under consideration. It however held that such arc carbonons were covered by Entry No. 4 of the 1st Schedule of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. The High Court dismissed the appeal without taking further evidence. In these appeals by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the goods under consideration are covered by Item No.4 of the first schedule to the Andhra pradesh General Sales tax Act, and therefore, they fall under Entry No., 4 of Schedule 1 of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The term "accessories" is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. A sense in which the word accessory is used is given in Webster 's Third New International Dictionary as follows: "all objects or device that is not essential in itself but that adds to the beauty, convenience or effectiveness of something else". Other meanings given there are: "supplementary or secondary to something of greater or primary importance", "additional"; "any of several mechanical devices that assist in operating or controlling the tone resources of an organ." "Accessories" are not necessarily confined to particular machines for which they; may serve as aids. The same item may be an accessory of more than one kind of instrument. It will be noticed that the entry shows that some precision has been attempted in making the entries. When it was intended to confine the entry to particular gadgets and "parts thereof" the entry said so. Of course, even where an entry relates to parts manufactured for Use for a particular kind of instruments of gadget only, the article, manufactured to serve as a part of a particular type of instrument would not cease to be covered under the intended Entry simply because a purchaser makes some other use of it. [564B C] 2. The Andhra Pradesh High Court correctly held that the main use of the arc car bons under consideration was duly proved to be that of production of powerful light used in projectors in cinemas. The fact that they can also be used for search lights, signalling stage lighting or where powerful lighting for photography or other purposes may be required, could not detract from the classification to which the carbon arcs belong. That is determined by their ordinary or commonly known purpose or user. This, as already observed by us, is evident from the fact that the appellants are known as 'cinema are carboons in the market.

Section 15 of the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules, 1966 empowers the Central Government to enhance or reduce the rate of royalty prescribed by the Second Schedule in respect of any mineral subject to the condition that the Central Govern ment shall not enhance the rate Of royalty in respect thereof of any minor mineral more than once during any period of three years. Section 14 of the Act provides that sections 5 to 13 (inclusive) shall not apply to quarry leases, mining leases or other mineral concessions in re spect of minor minerals and for purposes connected therewith. Clause (e) of the said section defines 'minor minerals ' as building stones, gravel, ordinary clay, ordinary sand other than sand used for prescribed purposes and any other mineral which the Central Govt may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare to be a minor mineral. It is not disputed that Black Trap and Hard Murrum are notified as minor minerals. The Act has made provision with regard to the issue of prospecting licences and mining leases in respect Of minor minerals which are won by the mining lease holders under the Act at the rates prescribed in the Second schedule to the Act. Under section 3A of the the Act the word 'minerals ' is defined as including all minerals except mineral oils. Clause 2(vi)(a) defines "minor minerals" as building stone stones, ravel, normal clay, sand other then sand used or for prescribed purpose and any further mineral which is the Central Gov ernment may, from time to time by notification, in the official Gazette, specify. Rule 21 of the Rules provides that a holder of a mining lease granted under the Rules shall pay royalty at the rate prescribed for the time being in the rules framed by the State Government in respect o f minor minerals provided in column 2 of the Schedule removed or consumed by him or by his agent, manager, employee, contractor or sub lessee from the leased area at the scales specified against them in column 3 of the schedule. Rule 22 provides that no royalty shall be charged from Nimbhadas of village potters if their annual produc tion is not exceeding two lakh bricks and they supply at least one lakh bricks to the Rural Housing Board or Panchayats. The validity of rule 21 as it existed prior to the issuance of the impugned notification was considered in B.K. Trivedi & Sons and Ors. vs State of Gujarat and Ors., [1989] 4 S.C.C., Judgments Today 190 that the royalty levied and covered under the rules should be applied only for mineral development and since the said royalty is being treated as part of the consolidated fund of the State and used for other purposes by the state, the levy was bad. The petitioners in these petitions challenged the validity of Rule 21 which was substituted in the place of the former rule 21 by a new rule which reads thus: "21. Rate of royalty in case of specified minor minerals has been enhanced from Rs.4 to Rs.7 per metric tonne. The contention of the petitioners was that under Entry 50 of List II of the 7th Schedule to the Constitution, the royalty recovered by the Govern ment had to be used only for minerals and could not be used for any other purpose. According to them the Act had been passed for purposes of regulation and development of minerals. They relied on the language of Entry 50 which reads as follows: "taxes on mineral rights subject to any limitations imposed by Parliament by law relating to mineral development" and contended that the levy in question was in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The levy is made under a law made by the Central Legislature on which alone the restriction contemplat ed under Article 304(b) applies.

The appellant was elected as a trustee by the Sengunatha Mudaliars of Manjakollai village at a meeting held on June 27, 1957. According to the appellant the temple was rounded two hundred years ago by the members of his community and since then the management of the temple and is affairs was always vested in the community of the Sangunatha Ammal Community and no person other than the elected trustee had at any time the right of management and control of the Temple. The Commissioner of Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments, Madras held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee and the suit was not barred by limitation. The respondents took the matter in appeal to the Madras High Court which allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the Subordinate Judge Nagapattinam. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) that the succession is "regulated by usage", and (ii) that according to the usage of the deity the trustees were elected for a period of one year each at a meet of the members Of the Sangunatha Mudaliar Community and so the appellant must be held to be a trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Madras Act 19 of 1951. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1)(a) The word "succession" in relation to property and rights and interests in property generally implies "passing of an interest from one person to another". [431C] (b) It is not possible to say that there was a succession of As office to another when on the efflux of the period for which A was appointed, there is a vacancy and B is elected to that vacancy. It is quite possible that for that vacancy A himself might be reelected because a retiring trustee is eligible for reelection. The possibility of A being the successor A himself is not merely an anomaly, it is an impossible legal position. No man can succeed to his own office. [432D E] (c) In the present case there is no warrant for this argument. The phrase "regulated By usage" in section 6 (9) would include even such cases. But the election to the office of trustee in the present ease is for a fixed period of time and not for life.

The appellant was the village Munsif (Headman). On April 26, 1971 at about 10.00 P.M., he was sleeping on a bench outside his cattle shed in the open space, which is shown in the site plan (exhibit P15) at No. 9. The younger brother of the deceased, Pandurangam woke up at about 11.15 p.m. On hearing the shout of his deceased brother crying "younger brother", he ran to his elder brother who came from the side of the bench where he was sitting and fell down on the southern side of a sluice of the north Boothagudi channel, which was shown at No 5 in the place plan (Exhibit P 15). The electric lights were burning in the vicinity He also saw two persons running ahead of accused Karunakaran. He further saw his two brothers, Gnanasakaran (PW 1) and Thiru gnanasambandam (PW 3) along with Ramasamy (PW 2), chasing them. He ran to their elder brother whom came from behind. The electric light were burning. He also seen the two accused running ahead. He was asked to lodge information at the police station which he did. On the prayer of the prosecution, the case against the first two accused without absconding accused was taken up for trial. The two accused were charged under section 120B read with sections 302 and 109 I.P.C. as well as under section 302/34 IPC. The case was referred to the High Court as usual and the accused also preferred appeals against their conviction and sentence. The High Court acquitted the second accused, Jabamani Nadar alias Kanyakumari Comrade alias Ramu and accepted the reference in respect of the present accused. His appeal was also dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. It is not possible to adopt that course in this case where the testimony of the sole witness has been rejected with reference to the first accused who was on the same boat with the appellant. The very fact that this eye witness could be persuaded to substitute PWs 1, 2 and 3 for his deceased younger brother as chasing the assailants, degrades him from the status of an absolutely reliable witness. He is definitely an obliging witness and cannot at all be trustworthy. This witness may not have a qualm of conscience in implicating the accused for the mere asking by someone, if not by the inimical police officer (PW 23) against whom criminal cases were pending at the instance of the accused 's father. Apart from that we find that the High court has not considered the intrinsic quality of the evidence of PW 4. It failed to notice certain broad facts which should definitely weigh with the Court while appreciating ocular testimony. From the medical evidence it is clear that there were more than one assailant and yet for the FIR it appears that there was only one assailant. This may not, in a given case, be considered as a very serious infirmity since the witness might not have seen the other. assailants when he came running to the place of occurrence. But the fact that the witness has stated in the first information report that the deceased was only mentioning the name of accused Damodaran as his assailant, this earlier version appears to be contradicted by the medical ' evidence. Besides, he has deliberately changed his own stand in court when he deposed that he saw two other persons running away after the assault is true, it is difficult to appreciate that he would not mention about this fact in the First Information Report. He admitted in the course of cross examination that the Sub Inspector asked him whether he had any witnesses and that he "did not tell about them due to excitement".

The respondents were partners in a firm of solicitors. Amarchand died on July 7, 1949. Thereafter the partnership was carried on by Mangaldas and Hiralal up to November 30, 1949, and on December 1, 1949 Ramesh son of Amarchand who had by then qualified as a solicitor joined the firm as the third partner. After the death of Amar Chand the arrangement between the various partners in regard to the realisations of the old outstandings was that in respect of the work done up to the death Of Amarchand the real receipts were to be divided amongst Amarchand, Mangaldas, Hiralal and Ramesh. The firm kept its accounts on cash basis. For the five assessment years 1950 51 to 1954 55 the respondents claimed that they had been assessed to income tax in the hands of the heirs and legal representatives just as the deceased Amarchand would have been had he not died. The Income tax Officer sought to tax these realisations but the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the notice under section 34 could validly be served only for the assessment years 1951 52, 1952 53, 1953 54 and 1954 55. On appeal by the respondents the Appellate Tribunal held that on a correct interpretation of section 24B the amounts which were received by the heirsand legal representatives after his death should be deemed by the fiction incorporated in sub section (1) to be income received by Amarchand and liable to tax under section 24 B(1) of the Income tax Act. On reference the High Court held that apart from section 24E of the Act the amounts were not taxable and that the section had no application to the case. Held, further, that on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the sums which are sought to be taxed and which have been held not to be liable to taxation are those which were not received in the previous year and are therefore not liable to be assessed as income (1), 244 Ellis C. Reid vs Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City, , referred to.

Section 3 of the Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Rules, 1959 gave power to make rules in respect of certain classes of employment in certain areas. The petitioners who were working in various offices located in the cities of Hyderabad and Secunderabad challenged the Act and the proposed action as ultra vires the Constitution. Their case was that Article 16(3) under which the Act, and the Rules purport to be made had been misunderstood as conferring a power to making, a law prescribing requirement as to residence in a part of a State. For this reason section 3 Of the Act was challenged as ultra rites. Held: (i) The word 'State ' here is to be understood in the extended use given to it by the definition of that word article 12. The second clause then specifies a prohibition against discrimination only on the grounds of religion, race, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or any of them. The intention here is making every office or employment open and available to every citizen, and inter alia to make offices or employment in one part India open to citizens in all other parts of India. (ii) The clause thus enables Parliament to make a law in a special case prescribing any requirement as regards residence within the State or Union territory prior to appointment, as a condition of employment, in the State and to remove ambiguity in language. 120 (iii) There can be no discrimination among other things on the ground of residence. Realising, however that sometimes local sentiments may have to be respected or sometimes an inroad from more advance States into less developed States might have to he prevented, and a residential qualification may, therefore, have to been prescribed, the exception in clause (3) was made. Even so, that clause speaks of residence within tho State. The claim for supremacy of Parliament is misconceived. Par liament in this case as in other matters, is supreme only in so far as the Constitution makes it. Where the Constitution does not concede supremacy, Parliament must act within its appointed functions and not transgress them. What the Constitution says is a matter for,construction of the language of the Constitution which is the proper construction of the two suggested? By the first clause equality of opportunity in employment or appointment to an office is guaranteed. By the second clause there can be any discrimination among others on the basis of residence or its duration rather than its location within the state. (iv) The claim of Mr. Setalvad that Parliament can make a provision regarding residence in any particular part of the State would render the general prohibition lose all its meaning.

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr post office. He was tried for offences under section 52 of the Post Office Act, 1898 and in two of them he was charged with offences under sections 467 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court acquitted the appellant but convicted him in each of the three appeals for offences tinder section 52. On appeal by the State it was contended that the search was illegal inasmuch as it was in contravention of the provisions of sections 103 and 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Held, that the prosecution had failed to prove that these letters were in the exclusive possession of the appellant. The mere fact that there is even a delay of several months in delivering a postal article to the addressee would not mean that the article had ceased to be in course of transmission. It is common experience that delivery of postal articles is now and again delayed for a considerable length of time may be through accident or through the negligence of the postal employees. It was probably for this reason that the definition clearly lays down that until an article despatched by post is delivered or can be said to be delivered that it will be deemed to be In course of trans portation by post from the time of its being delivered to a Post Office to the time when its being actually delivered to the sender or otherwise disposed of under Chapter VII. The object of the provision was to prevent postal articles 'in course of the transmission by post 'from being tampered with, and so the secreting, destruction etc., of postal article would frustrate or tend to frustrate their delivery to the addressees.

The appellants were alleged to have been abused and threatened by the Respondent that he should be laboured and his property worth about Rs. 40/ which was damaged. On September 2, 1963, the respondent filed an application under section 85 of the U.P. Panchayat Raj Act, 1947 against the appellants and section K. Srivastava for being impleaded as a party to the writ petition in the High Court. The High Court stayed further proceedings before the Nyaya Panchayat but on December 23, 1963 a notice was issued to the five members of that Bench to assemble on December 25, 1963 and they were heard by the respondent, who refused to take it. This fact was denied and the High court held that the respondent had knowledge of the order and that the order was passed deliberately to pass it to pass the order of the High 'Court. In appeal by special leave: HELD: (i) The High High Court did not appreciate that the so called affidavit which was filed before the Panchas was in fact not an affidavit at all. It had not been sworn to before any person authorised to administer oaths. It was no part of the duty of the Pan chachas to enquire from the S.D.M about the filing of the application before him. At any rate he had apparently no jurisdiction to stay proceedings before them. It is true that in certain cases proceedings can be adjourned to enable the parties to file better proof, but a judicial officer is not bound to do so and if he bona fide does not in his discretion adjourn it, he cannot be said that he has committed contempt of court. [120 F G; 120 B D E] (ii)The High Court while dealing with the evidence had not kept in mind the principles which we have mentioned above.

The appellant was charged with murder of a person who was sleeping in his cattle shed in village Bhadurpur Ghar, with a sword at about mid night on the night between June 14 15, 1960. The prosecution case was that due to enmity, the appellant caused injuries to Sheo Sahai and asked him to go to the Police Station, Ekdil, nine miles away and lodged a report. He delivered the sword which had been found by the Serologist to be stained with human blood. The appellant was taken in custody and as a result of investigation was sent up for trial, The appellant denied the allegation that he had caused the death of Sheo Sahai. The Sessions Judge believed Ujagar Singh 's statement about the appellant 's confessing to him that he did commit the murder of Sheo Swarup Sahai and that he deposited it stained with his human blood at the Police station on the day of the murder. The High Court, however, did not rely on this extra judicial confession. It relied on certain statements made by the appellant in his report dictated at the police Station and considered those facts together with the motive and the evidence about the purchase of the sword sufficient to confirm the appellant his conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the entire report dictated by the appel lant was inadmissible in evidence as its contents amounted to a confession of the offence by the accused made to a Police Officer and that the evidence relied upon by the High Court was insufficient to establish conclusively that the appellant had murdered Sheo Sahai, and that there were good reasons for Ujagar Singh not leaving his field whose crops he was watching against the neel gais. HELD: (i) The extra judicial confessions are not usually considered with favour but that does not mean that such a confession coming from a person whom who has no reason to state falsely and to whom it is made in circumstances which tend to support his statement should not be believed. [206 E] (ii) It may be that having blurted out the truth to be proceeded to the police station and report the matter there, there is no reason for a person 's acting in a certain manner. It may also be that taking blurtling out the falsehood to Ujagar Singh, when taken by surprise, the appell lant thought the best thing to be to proceed to the nal police station, and report about it.

The appellant, a Municipal Corporation of Raipur published the preliminary electoral roll on September 30, 1978 under Rule 4(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Munici pal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication of Electoral Rolls and Selection of Councillors) Rules 1963. The Collector published the final electoral roll under Rule 8 of the Rules on November 16, 1978 notifying that the poll, if necessary, would take place on December 31, 1978 in all the 44 constituencies: Six petitioners including the appellants presented a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur on December 28, 1978 requesting the court to make an order quashing the electoral roll and the calendar of events issued for the purpose of the said election and directing the respondents not to notify the results of the election under Rule 46 of the rules pending disposal of the petition. The writ petition itself was filed on December 29, 1978 when the poll had to take place in all 44 constituencies; six petitioners including appellants presented their claim and that the applications were disposed of on October 30,1978. The Deputy Collector rejected the claims and objections made by the appellants. Thereafter the successful candidates were also impleaded as respondents and the petition was amended by inclusion of an additional prayer that the declaration of results of all the 43 successful candidates should also be quashed. After the respondents filed their counter affidavits, the petition being heard and it was dismissed by a Division Bench of the High court on January 20, 1979. The appellants thereupon filed a writ petition in the High Courts challenging the validity of the electoral rolls and the declaration thereof of results. The learned Single Judge before whom the case came up for orders directed the issue of notice of the petitions and the stay application to the respondents and issued an interim order directing the respondent not to publish the results. On December 31. 1978, the poll was held and 44 persons were declared elected. Their names were, however, not published under Rule 56 of the Munichi pal Corporation Rules in view of the interim order made by this Court. Thereafter, the successful candidate were also included as respondents. The petition was filed in December 1979 for a writ of certiorari quashing the election proceedings on the ground that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule (1) Of the Rules notifying that claims and objection should be preferred within 30 days from the date of publication of that notice when sub rule (3) of Rule 4 of the Act prescribed that such claims and/or objections could be preferred. The Division Bench dismissed the writ petition on January 21, 1979 holding that the petitioners were not prompt in moving the High courts after undue delay. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The final electoral rolls were published on November 25, 1978 and it is only on December 5, 1978 for the first time that a letter was addressed by petitioner No. 6 to the Collector drawing his attention to the error that had crept into the notice published under rule 4(i) of Rules. The final list of candidates for the election with their symbols was published on December 20, 1978.

The respondent company and its directors were prosecuted under sections 32(5) and 133(3) of the Companies Act, 1913 for failure to Me with the Registrar of Companies on or before 30 10 1967 the balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company as required under section 220(1) of that Act. The High Court acquitted the directors holding that if no balance sheet was laid before a general body meeting nor could it be so laid, there can be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted nor of complying with the requirements of section 220 and though wilful omission to call a general Body meeting and lay the balance sheets and profit & loss account before it may expose the person responsible to punishment under other provisions of the Act, it certainly does not make him liable under the provisions of section 134(4) of Companies Act 1913 or section 220 of the . In appeal by special leave, HELD : (1) The holding of the annual general meeting and the laying before it of the balancesheet and profit account is a sine qua non for filing of the copies thereof before the Registrar. If no such balance sheet is laid before the general body, there could be no objection to that balance sheets not being utilised nor of compliance with the provisions contained in any of the four preceding sub sections. [416 A] (2) The finding of the High Court that section 26 makes the offence a continuing one also shows that the obligation to file the list is independent of the holding of a general meeting. [417 B C] (3) Under section 134 the laying of a balance sheet or profit and losses account before the company in the general meeting is made obligatory. Under section 133 the failure to comply with section 131 is made punishable. But section 134 lays down that after balance sheet, and profit loss account or the income and expenditure account as the case may be, have been laid before it at a general Meeting three copies thereof shall be filed with the registrar, and a failure to do so is made penal by the Act. [414 C] Gibson vs Barlon, ; , followed. (4) The liability of sending three copies of the Balance sheet and profits and loss accounts which are laid before such general body may have been forwarded under sub section (1), of section 132 cannot be complied with. While the appeal to a question of principle might be attractive, it cannot ignore the clear words of the section. Where the words of a section are very clear it is unnecessary to consider whether it embodies any principle and whether that principle is consistent with the principle as embodied a certain other sections which are differently worded. In interpreting a penal provision it is not permissible to give an extended meaning to the plain words of that section on the ground that a principle recognised in respect of certain other provisions Of law requires that this section should be interpreted is the same way. [413 D E] (5) The court there observed that the decision in Park vs Lawton, ; and Park vs lawton, , referred to.

The respondent and 49 other persons were charged with various offences alleged to have been committed by them in the course of their raid as an armed gang on a certain factory known as the Jessop Factory at Dum Dum, and they were convicted and sentenced to varying terms of imprison ment by the Special Court to which the case was sent for trial by the Governor of West Bengal by a notification dated 26th January 1950. The respondent applied to the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the conviction and sentence on the ground that the Special judge had no jurisdiction to try the case inasmuch as section 5 (1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1949, was discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitu tion in so far as it purported to vest in the State Government an absolute and arbitrary power to refer to a special court for trial "any cases ", which must include an individual case, "whether the duration of such a case is likely to be long or not ". The High Court quashed the conviction. Held, that section 5(1) Of the WestBengal Special Courts Ordinance, 1949 was valid as it did not by itself make any distinction between cases and offences triable by the special court and those for the purpose of being tried by a Special Court. The classification implied in this part of the sub section had no reference to, and was not directed towards the singling out of any particular person as an object of hostile State action but was concerned only with the grouping of "offences", "classes of offences" and "cl classes of cases".

The appellant was appointed as a Lecturer in Radiology in Maulana Azad Medical College, New Delhi. By letter dated April 6, 1965 the Delhi Administration informed the Principal, Maulana Gandhi Medical College that the Vice Chancellor of the Delhi University in exercise of his emergency powers had granted him recognition as an Associate Professor of Radiotherapy for teaching the post graduate and under graduate students for the D.M.R.T. and M.B.S. courses of studies. The appellant was called by the Banaras Hindu University for an interview on August 7, 1972 for the post of Professor of radiotherapy but since the post was falling vacant in 1973 he did not appear for the interview. The Government of India Ministry of Health and Family Planning Department of Health by its letter dated February 23, 1974 informed the Delhi Adminis tration that it was not possible to relieve the appellant of his duties or place his services on deputation with a lien on his post as Radiologist in the Irwin Hospital. The Ministry of Finance by its Letter dated January 17, 1976 however informed the Secretary (Medical), Delhi Administration that it had no objection to designating him as Associate Professor and that the appellant could not be considered for appointment to the post. In response to an advertisement of the Union Public Service Commission for the non teaching post of Radiologist, the appellant was asked by the Government to give up all connections with the Central Health Service. The letter further stated that the Government had no objections to designing him as a Associate Professor or Radiology (ex officio) in the Maulana New Azad Medical 25 College provided it was neither detrimental to his normal duties as a Radiologist nor any financial implications were involved. The respondent State of Punjab by its order dated January 9, 1979 informed the appellant that the post had fallen vacant in 1974 and that consequent upon the appointment of the appellant in Category `C ' of the Central health Service, the Administration had no objec tions to designate him as Assistant Professor. The order was challenged before the High Court which dismissed the writ petition holding that since the appellant had the essential qualification prescribed for teaching post the teaching experience gained by him while holding the post he held the post in the senior scale who had rendered not less than six years of service in that speciality and 20% of the vacancies thereof were to be filled by direct recruitment in the manner specified in the Second Schedule, he was clearly eligible for appointment as Professor or radiology in the Medical College. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The post of Assistant Professor of Pathology (Ex officio) is a post belonging to Specialist Grade I which is equivalent to Supertime Grade II carrying a pay scale of Rs. 8(3) provides that 50% of vacancies in super time grade II to be filling in by promotion of General Duty Officers Grade I and Specialists Grade II officers in the ratio of 2 :3 and the remaining 50% Of the vacancies to be carried filled by promotion through Departmental Promotion Committee of officers holding the posts in the junior scale who have rendered not more than six year ' teaching experience out of 12 years ' standing in the grade through the Union Government Public Service Commis sion. [27A B] 2. The qualifications and experience prescribed in Annexure I to the Second schedule determine the question of his eligibility for such promotion or appointment.

The workmen of Orient Paper Mills Ltd., Brajrajnagar, have come up in this appeal by special leave against an award of the Industrial Tribunal, Orissa. The dispute related to fixation of wages including minimum wages and this was covered by items Nos. 1, 3, 4, 22 and 26 in the Schedule attached to the order of reference. The Tribunal gave its award on all the thirty items. The special leave in this Court was sought and granted in respect of two matters covering some of these items. In the course of arguments before this Court it was contended that (1) the Tribunal committed an error in fixing the minimum wage in the Company on the basis of the average minimum wages prevailing in other industries in that region, and (2) the principle laid down by this Court in French Motor Car Co. vs Its Workmen ; , followed. Held: (i) The Tribunal committed no error in arriving at this decision and consequently the total minimum wage fixed by it must also be deemed to have the same break up. As a result of the award, the Tribunal was entitled to fix the minimum wages in the company on the principle contained in the earlier Agreement of the parties and in holding that there was no justification for departing from the figure of Rs.95 which is the average Minimum wage payable by those industries (1 ) [1963] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 673, followed. (ii) The award had to cover the year 1963 64 also and at least for that year the accounts could not possibly have been completed as that year was still running when the award was given by the Tribunal on the 11th January, 1964.

The material portion of that notice reads as follows "Notice under section 149 of the I.T.O. 30 4 66. Whether it is a new case or one in which re assessment (or recomputation) has to be made Re assessment 5. If a case of reassessment (or Computation) the income (or loss or depreciation allowance originally assessed/determined. Rs. 73,604/ 6. Whether the case falls under cl. (a) or (b) of section 148 147(A) 7. The Income tax Officer issued to him a notice containing all or any of the requirements which may be included in a notice. Section 25(4) of the Income tax Act, 1922, provides that where any business, profession or vocation on which tax was at any time charged under the provisions of the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1939, is discontinued, then unless there has been a succession by virtue of which the provisions Of sub section (4) have been rendered applicable no tax shall be payable in respect of the income, profits and gains of the period between the end of the previous year and the date of such discontinuance. Section 25(3) provides that the business must have been charged to tax under the Indian Incometax Act, 1918. The appellant claimed relief under section 25(1) contending that it had transferred its business to a limited company with effect either from November 13, 1947 or February 13, 1948, by an instrument executed on February 7, 1948. The claim was rejected by the Income Tax Officer and by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and also by the Incometax Appellate Tribunal on appeal to this Court. HELD: (i) Under section 25 (4), a mere change in the constitution of the partnership does not count and sections 25(2) and 26 (2) do not apply at the same time, because the intention is obviously to keep them separate and when sub section 4 was added, sub section 3 was amended by the addition of the words "unless there has already been a devolution by virtue Of which the provi sions of sub section 2 have been made applicable. The business which had been subjected to tax in 1939 had been discontinued in October/November 1937 or on May 30, 1939 and it was not in existence in 1948 so as to permit a succession to it taking place under the instrument of February 7. [108 E F] (ii) Under sub section(4), the business could be said to have ceased. The income tax Act does not in terms of joint family business but in terms Of business in a business sense, and it is the business which was taxed under the Act of 1918 which must cease to exist before the benefit of section 25 can be obtained. It is possible that the decision might be justified on the ground that the benefit was being claimed by one of the members of the erstwhile family and not by the whole family, though I express no opinion upon it, but even so that would be a case of succession rather than of discontinuance. The Madras case cannot, however, be made applicable to the present facts because, as pointed out already by me, there was no cessation of business in so far as the original business of piece goods, yarn and banking was concerned.

The appellant 's suit based as it was on the provisions of section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, was essentially a claim to obtain a share in the interest which her husband had at the time of his death in the coparcenary property. Two things became necessary to determine for the purpose of giving relief to the plaintiff. One, her share in her husband 's share and two, her husband, 's own share in a coparcenary property, were thus clears : One, that in a partition between Khandappa and his two sons, there would be four sharers in the joint family properties, the fourth being Khandappa 's wife, the plaintiff 's son, and their two children each having a 1/4th share therein. Adding 1/3rd and 1/24th, the appellant claims a 7/24 th share in one of the joint families. The other three getting 1/2 share each would devolve upon his death on six sharers, the other being Khandappappa ' 's 1/6th share would devolve on his death. On the question whether the plaintiff was entitled to a 7 /24th share by ignoring the 1/5th share which she would have obtained had there been a partition during her husband life time between him and his sons. HELD : (1) The view taken by the Bombay High Court in Rangubai Lalji vs Laxman Lalji, [1959] Stipp. 1 S.C.R. 394, that Explanation 1 to section 6 does not apply, that the proviso to that section is attracted and that the decision of the appeal must turn on the meaning to be given to Explanation 1 of section6. The interpretation which will further the intention of the legislature and remedy the injustice from which the Hindu women have suffered over the years, is truly to permit one 's imagination to boggle under the oppression of the reality that there was in fact no partition between the plaintiff and his coparceners immediately before his death, and that assumption, having been made once for the purposes of ascertaining the share of the deceased in the coparcener property, one cannot go back on that assumption and ascertain the share Of the heirs without reference to it. [765 E F] (2) The plain meaning of Explanation 1 is the subject matter of acute controversy between the parties. The plaintiff ' s suit based on the provision of section 30 of the Act was essentially one claim to recover a share from the defendant. The proviso to section six comes into play and the normal rule is excluded. [766 G] (3) The interpretation that Explanation I has to be read as enabling a person who has separated himself from the coparcenary before the death of the person in whose property the heirs claim a share. The fiction created by Explanation 1 has to he given its due and full effect as the fiction created under section 18A(9)(b). [767 A] (4) The assumption that Explanation1 has to have been given its true effect is not a processual step devised merely for the limited purpose of working out some other conclusion. It has to, be treated and accepted as a concrete reality, something that cannot be recalled just as a share allotted to a coparcener in an actual partition cannot generally be recalled.

The Life Insurance Corporation of India (Staff) Regulations, 1960 were brought into force with effect from 27.7.60. Prior to January, 1955 there were more than 200 insur ers carrying on life insurance business in India. As it came to the notice of the Government that the Indian life insur tors, with a few exceptions, were virtually controlled by few individuals who were utilising the funds of those companies to the detriment of the industry and the policyholders, the Govern ment decided to nationalise the life insurance busi ness. Accordingly the President of India promulgated the Life Insurance (Emergency Provisions) Ordi nance, 1956 on January 19, 1956 providing for the vesting of the management of the life Insurance business (which was called the controlled business under the Ordinance which was being carried on by any insurer in India on that day in the Central Government and providing for its management. According to section 11(2) of the Act, the Central Govern ment may, notwith standing anything contained in sub section (1), or in any other law for the time being in force, alter (whether by way of reduction or otherwise) the remuneration and conditions of service applicable to employees or any class of them is called for, the. Central Government might, if it is of the opinion that it was in the interest of the Corporation to do so, direct such employee to retire on completion of 50 years of age or at any time thereafter on giving him three months ' notice or salary in lieu thereof. There will be no distinction between class 111 and Class IV employees recruited to the service of the Corpora tion after 1st September 1956 by making amendments in section 11 (2) read as follows: " Section 11(1) provides that where the Central Govt. is satisfied that for the purpose of securing uniformity in the scales of remuner ation and the other terms and conditions Of service applicable, to employees of insurers whose controlled business had been transferred to and vested in it or for the purposes of reducing the remu neration payable to those employees in cases where in the interests of the corporation and its policyholders a reduction in the remuneration payable, or a revision of the other term and conditions re quired shall be called for. " The first proviso provides that notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in sub sections (1) and (2), the Central Gov ernment may, by order, made by the Central Gover ment, direct ed such employee, to retire after completion of 55 years of service or at a time thereafter, on giving notice of termination. Section 11 (3) provides for the premature retirement of an employee belonging to Class I or Class II categories appointed to the serv ice of the Corpo ration on or after 1th September, 1956.

The appellants wrote a letter to the President of India with copies to others with the sole object of conveying the opinion that the public expression by the Hon 'ble Judge of his personal views on controversial matters con cerned the merits and demerits of the present system of Government was not in keeping with the well accepted role of proverbial aloofness of a Judge. The letter stated that Justice D.S. Tewatia of the Punjab and Haryana High Court visited the session division of Bhiwani and inspected the Courts from 14 February 1975 to 19 February 1975. In that letter they also brought to the notice of the President that Justice S.D. Tewar, Bhiwani had visited the courts and inspected them on 17 February 1975 and thereafter stated as follows: "The learned Judge met the members of the Bar on 15 February, 1975 in the Bar Room, Bhiwwani. During the course of his discussion with the members, he discussed politics with them and criticised the present executive in general and the Congress Party in particular. He also enquired all about Shri Sohan Lal a leader of the teacher 's movement in the State". The letter concluded by saying that the Honble Judge during his entire stay in his tour deliberately showed the bent of his mind towards commu nism while exchanging view on various matters. The appellants took a copy of their letter to Chief Justice of Punjab andHaryana High Court, the Chief Minister of Haryana and the Prime Minister. In reply they said that the contents of the letter were not correct. They also stated that the letters written by the appellants were correct. It was intended to be a privileged communication made solely with a view to uphold the dignity of the Court. The deponent has been taught to believe that a Judge ought always to steer clear of all avoidable controversial matter. The High Court did not mention which particular portion of the said letter constituted contempt of court. It is an article of faith with the deponent that dignity and respect of all Courts and of all Judges particularly of the High Court must be maintained for, amongst other reasons on that depends the orderly function ing of the society as also prestige of the profession to which the deponent has the honour to belong. The deponents stated that if the Court is of the view that the letter of the deponents constitute for any reason contempt of Court, no one would be more sorry than the deponent himself. Therefore, the deponent tenders his apology to this Hon ' ble Court for the same and prays for its acceptance." The appellants filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the maintainability of the contempt petition contending that the allegations in the letter amounted to scandalising the Hon`ble Judge or the Court in any manner to weaken people 's faith in the administration of justice. The petition was dismissed by the Full Bench. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (1) that there was no intention whatsoever on his part to scandalise the Hon"ble Judge, or this Hon ble Court or to lower the authority or undermine the prestige of his learned Judge or of the Hon ble court or to weak in any way the confidence of the people in the adminis tration of justice; (2) that the communication did not bear out any foundation for an action for criminal contempt. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1(a) The letter does not interfere much less substantial ly with due course of justice or proper administration of law by the courts. [246E] (b) It will not be correct and proper for any Judge to accept the invitation and hospitality of any busi ness or commercial organisation or of any political party or of a group or organisation run on sectarian, communal or parochial lines.

The petitioner company was a company registered under the Indian Companies Act. Suraj Mall Mohta was also the managing director of another company Messrs. Jute and Gunny Brokers Ltd. A reference had been made by the Central Government under section 5(1) of the Act before 58 450 1st September, 1948, of the case of the petitioner along with the cases of Suraj Mall Keta and other members of his family may be referred to the Commission for investigation. On the 15th of September, 1953, a report to this effect was made by it to the Central Govern ment under section 6(1), requesting that the case be investigated and they were called upon to furnish certain material as detailed in Annexure "B" of the petition, to the petitioner. On 12th April 1954, the Commission notified the petitioners that their cases had been referred for investigation and they should furnish certain materials as detailed therein. The present petition under article 32 of the Constitution was filed for the issue of appropriate writs restraining the Commission from taking any action against the petitioner under the provisions of the , on the ground that the provisions Of sections 5(4), 6, 7 and 8 of the Indian Income tax Act had become void being discriminatory in character after the coming into force of the constitution of India. Held, that section 5 (1) Of the Indian Incometax Act and sub section (4) of section 5 of the impugned Act deal with all persons who have similar characteristics and similar properties, the common characteristics being that they are persons who had not truly disclosed their income and have evaded payment of taxation on income. It is not possible to hold that all such persons who evade payment of income tax and come within the ambit of section 34 of the Income tax ' Act and come under it, but without in any way deciding or even expressing any opinion on that question, they cannot be dealt with under the provi sions of section 4 Of the impugned act. The procedure thus prescribed by the impugned provisions is substantially prejudicial to the assessee than the procedure prescribed under the Act.

The respondent, a company registered under section 26 of the Indian Companies Act 1913, was carrying on business in matters of inland and foreign trade. The primary objects of the Federation as given in the Memorandum of Association are "regulation of hours of work, payment of wages, leave, holiday terms of service and other conditions of work of persons employed in shop commercial establishment, establishments for public entertainment or amusement and other establishments and to provide for certain matters connected therewith". Section 1(4) indicates its extent and application. It shall apply in the first instance only to the municipal areas, notified areas of Delhi and New Delhi etc., but Government may by notification extend or apply it to shops and establishments in the other local area or areas. The definitions of " commercial establishment" and "shop" given in sub sections (5), (9) and (27) of section 2 are material for our purpose. They read " Commercial Establishment" means any premises wherein any trade, business or profession is carried on, or (b) any work in connection with, or incidental or ancillary thereto is carried On and includes a society registered under the , and charitable or other trust, whether registered or not which carries on any business, trade or profession. " Establishment" mean any premises where goods are sold, either by retail or wholesale Or where services are rendered to customers, and includes an office, a stoic room, godown, warehouse or work place, whether in the same premises or otherwise used in connection therewith or in connection With such trade or business but does not include a shop or a factory registered under tho , or theaters, cinemas, restaurants eating houses, residential hotels, clubs or other places of public amusement or entertainment. " establishment" means a shop, a commercial establishment and a residential hotel, restaurant, eating house, theatre or other place of public entertainment to which this Act applies and includes such other establishment as Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare to be an establishment for the purposes of the Act. " Commercial establishment" is defined in section 2(5) of the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act, 1954. The main object of the said Act as stated in its preamble is "regulation for hours of business, payment, of wages etc., of persons engaged in shop, commercial establishments, establishments, for public institution or amusement or other establishments". Section 2(7) defines 'establishment ' to mean any building where goods were sold, whether by retail, wholesale or where services were rendered to customer. The definition of "commercial establishment" includes a shop and a commercial Establishment. The term "shops" is wide enough to include the idea of profit, yet the definition of the mere word "trade" does not necessarily mean something by which a profit is made. But putting aside the question whether they carry on a trade, how can it be denied that the Council carry on business. They are incorporated; they have a secretary and they print books, they sell those books, them do all that is ordinarily done in carrying on the business of a bookseller. The mere fact of the matter is that the respondent is a Federation of Federations and not an association of any individual traders, industrialists or businessmen. As regards the preliminary objection, it was held by this Court that the activity of the Association amounts to "work in connection" with, inter alia, of "industry" as defined in s.2(j) of ' the Act, which in consequence had no application. From the side of the present appellant, at first a half hearted attempt was made to show that the Federation is carrying on a profession as it is "tendering advice to all businessmen and traders". This contention was negatived by this court in Management of the Union of the India Chamber of Commerce and Industry vs Their workmen, Shri R. K. Mittal, [1971] 1 S.C.R. No. 869.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family headed by one Sri Trivikram Narain Singh who was the original founder and owner of what is known as Ausanganj State in the district of Benaras. By a Treaty between the East India Company Nawab Asfuddaula in or about the year 1775, the province of Benares was ceded to British Government. The British Government granted a sanad of Raj to Raja Chet Singh who in turn gave the Jagir of Parganas Seyedpur and Bhittery in perpetuity to Babu Har Narain Singh and his successors no longer remained the proprietors of the Parganas or the Jagir and became entitled to merely a pension. The letter by which the amount of pension was determined at Rs. 36,322/8 is dated July 7, 1837 and was from H. Elliot Esqr., the Secretary Sadar Board of Revenue N.W.P. Allahabad, to J. Thompson Esqrs., Offg. Secretary to Lt. Government, N. W.P., Allahabad, who held that the amount which had been received by the successors of Babu Harnarain Singh varied from year to year and did not fall within the category of agricultural income tax. The source of the pension was a liability undertaken by the Government for extinguishing the proprietary rights of the Jagirdar and when the immediate source of income was not land or rent collections from land, it is difficult to hold that the receipt of the assessee was agricultural income within the meaning of section 4(3)(viii) of the Income tax Act. The High Court held that from the language of the letter of July 7 1837 it was manifest that the right which was conferred was a right to a share of one fourth in the net land revenue collections after deducting costs of Tahsil establishment. It relied on the fact that the Government recouped this from the person with whom the land was settled, land in the genealogical tree of Malikana appears in the second degree, but the immediate and effective source is rent, which has suffered the accident of nonpayment. The allowance was in a sense related to the land revenue assessed on the land i.e., it was fixed as a percentage of the land Revenue; but the percentage was merely a measure, and indicated the source of this right in lieu of which the allowance was given. It was contended that if the assessee 's predecessor had received compensation for relinquishing his title to the lands in dispute, that would have been a capital receipt and not taxable. Held, further, that the allowance is revenue income and not exempt from taxation as agricultural income.

The appellants of the Civil Appeal No. 441 of 1981 claimed to have been appointed as Supervisors Grade 'A ' in various ordnance factories between 1962 to 1966 a nd had filed these writ petitions claiming that they had been appointed on various dates in pursuance of a circular dated 6th November, 1962 issued by the Director General of Ordnance Factories superseding h ises sion and in equiv a lent grades should be treated as follows: (i) All those Diploma holders who have been appoint ed as Supervisor 'B ' (Tech) or in equivalent grades for 2 years in Ordnance Factory should be promoted to Chargeman.
