The Karnataka State Transport Corporation, the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation and some other private operators filed writ petitions in this Court challenging the vires of section 63(7) of the . The High Court set aside the grant of three out of eleven permits to the Karnataka state Tourism Development Corporation and increased the number of permits granted to the Indian Tourism Development Corpora tion from one to three. The Tribunal took the view that having regard to the rule of preference enunciated by the proviso to section 63 (7), the applications from the 'non preferred ' category had to be excluded as the number Of applications from applicants who were required to be given preference exceeded the number specified in the proviso, and that the grant was set aside. The High court also took the same view. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of some of the private operators that the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the High Court were wrong in distinguishing the decision of this Court in Sher Singh 's case and that in the case of the court interpreted the word 'preference ' occurring in section 47(1 H) in the back ground of the provisions of Chapters IV and IV A of the Act, under the former of which the State transport Undertaking would have preference whereas under the latter the State Road transport Corporation would have a monopoly. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The general scheme of the Motor Vehicles Act in the matter of grant of permits for stage carriages and contract carriages appears to be that except in the cases of a notified route or notified area where under section 68 F(1) the permit has to be necessarily granted to tho State Transport Undertaking, in all other cases, the claims of all eligible applicants must be considered on merits, applying the rules of preference wherever the claims are approximately equal. The proviso to Section 47(I H) for example, provides that in case of inter State route, the Undertaking will have preference in the matters of stage carriage permit. [1015C D] 2. Clause (iv) of section 47 (1 H), for example provides that other conditions being equal, an application for a stage carriage permits from a cooperative society or a person holding a valid licence for driving transport vehicles shall as far as may be, be given priority over applications from individual owners. [ 1015E] 3. The word 'repreference" in section 2(25) is unconstitutional and it is not necessary that the department is able to exercise some control on the functioning of these operators. [10F] 4. Clause(iv) provides for a preference, not to operators of tourist vehicles but to operators or of tourist cars and travel agents. Though the permits to be granted are for tourist vehicles, the preference is confined to operators who of tourist car and travel agent. Although the permits are for Tourist vehicles, it mentions that approval carries with it certain privileges, such as allotment of ex STC vehicles and that it is, therefore, necessary that they should be owning and operating five vehicles as tourist taxies of either indigenous make or acquired from elsewhere regardless of the period in the car hire business or that they must be ex Defence Service personnel, who satisfy certain prescribed conditions. The matter appears to have been left to the total discretion of the Central Government, virtually as we said, pre empting the decision. [1005C E] Sher Singh vs Union of India, ; , referred to.

The respondent purchased, by a registered instrument dated October 5, 1956, the business carried on by one Purushottam Raju under the name All India Trading Company. Purushottam Raju was the sole proprietor of the business and had been assessed to sales tax in respect of his turnover for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. The assessee paid some amounts towards sales tax thus determined but there remained some arrears of sales tax i.e., Rs. 3836 4 0 for 1948 49, and Rs. 1218 1 9 for 1949 50 The Sales Tax authorities attempted to recover the arrears of tax from the respondent as the purchaser of the said business. The respondent 6 63 denied liability to pay sales tax but his contention was over ruled by the Deputy Commercial Tax Officer. The appellant then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the orders of the Commercial Tax officer and the Board of Revenue. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that Rule 21 A was ultra vires of the rule making power of the State Government under section 19(1) and (2) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The word 'assessment ' used in section 19 (2)(c) does not include the power of recovering tax assessed from a person other than the assessee. It follows therefore that Rule is beyond the rulemaking power of State Government either under section19(1), or section 19, (2). [665 B] Badridas Daga vs C.I.T., Bihar, ; Chatturam vs C I.T. Bihar, , Chattaram vs C., I. T. Bihar and Chattamuram vs Commissioner of Inland Revenue, A. 1. R. , referred to.

The appellant entered service in the Gondal State. In 1927, he was suspended and at that time he was acting as Accountant at Rajkot Central Prison, and on March 7, 1954, he had committed certain acts of mis appropriation of food stuffs meant for prisoners maltreatment of prisoners and acceptance of illegal gratification from them, but on enquiry held by him, the police found that the appellant 's conduct amounted to denial of reasonable opportunity contemplated by article 311(2) of the Constitution. The appellant 'reprehensible action taken against him in respect of arrears of pay from April 1, 1954 to May 7, 1956. He filed a written statement contending that the departmental enquiry was vitiated as he had not been furnished with copies of the report of the Enquiry Officer, and that the Inspector General of Prisons had recorded before him and the tentative conclusions arrived at by the Enquiry officer were bound to influence him, and in depriving them of a copy of the same he was handicapped. The High Court held that the failure on the part of the competent authority to provide the appellant with a copy, of the enquiry report amounted to violation of article 311 (2) Of the Constitution, as according to it there was no duty to supply a copy thereof and had not prejudiced by the non supply of the copy of his report. Held, that though some elements of relationship existed between a public servant and Government servants, the liability to pay wages when it has been fixed arises out of a contract to pay salary, is not lacking even in England where a special relationship exists between the Crown and its public servants. In the present case, however, some elements were of relationship which arose between the appellant and Government were based on contract within the meaning of section 60 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960, and the liability arising out of them was one of damages. The decree of the High Court decreeing payment of arrears was truly a liability in proceedings relating to a contract within section 60(2)(a) of that Act rather than under section 61.

The appellant was granted a lease of the coal and coal mining rights in respect of 400 bighas out of his total area. The lease deed provided that the northern boundary of the leasehold land was to be drawn between the two leaseholds. The western boundary was shown as the northern boundaries of the lease hold of Samanta. On June 15,1900, the appellant made an inquiry and came to know that the defendants had encroached upon their coal mines on the northern side and removed coal from the encroached portion and had rendered the remaining coal of the encroached portions unworkable. The Commissioner appointed by the Court tested the position of the six trijunction pillars shown in the map of lease dated November 23, 1900, and found that two of the trijram pillars were in their correct positions. On these allegations the appellant asked for the following reliefs: (a) That the intermediate boundary line between the appellants ' coal land and the defendants ' coal mining right be ascertained and fixed; (b)That a permanent injunction be issued against the defendants restraining them from encroaching upon the plaintiffs ' coal mines and removing coal therefrom. The respondents denied that they had encroached on the plaintiff ' coal lands and stated that the suit was barred by limitation. The trial court held that the defendant had encroached Upon the appellant 's coal land, that the lease deed was not a valid document and that the boundary could more satisfactorily be fixed with reference to the plans annexed to the subsequent lease deeds executed in favour of the successors in interest of the appellant and the respondents. On appeal the High Court accepted all the findings of the trial court and dismissed the appeal. Held: (i) The finding of the courts below that the disputed extent of land was part of the holding of the respondents, is vitiated by an error of law by the burden of proof having been wrongly thrown on the appellant. (ii) The onus was upon the plaintiff in these suits to prove that the knowledge of his father wag within three years of the suit and that is all. If he proves this, then to succeed in the plea of limitation the defendant has to prove satisfactorily that the fact that the property was in his possession became known to the plaintiff more than three years prior to the suit. (iii) The burden of proving that the title was in the possession of the defendant within three year of the date of filing of the suits, and that was all. , therefore, on the respondents it could not be held that they were guilty of any breach of contract.

The appellant, a saw mill in the State of Kerala, was in the employ of the appellant as a crosscutter. It was alleged that on June 21, 1958, Sankaran came drunk to them mill and abused them with physical violence. He was caught hold of by other workmen and taken outside. The appellant served a charge sheet on Sankaran on June 24, 1958 acting out the above facts and asked him to show cause why his services should not be terminated on account of his grave indiscipline and misconduct. Sankaran gave an explanation the same day denying the allegations of fact made against him though he admitted that he had come to the mill at the relevant time for taking his wages for that week. On July 8, 1958 Sankaran again wrote to the appellant to hold the inquiry as early as possible. On August 9, 1958 the appellant terminated the services of Sankaran under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders without holding any departmental enquiry and the order was communicated to Sankaran. The Industrial Tribunal held that something seemed to have happened on the afternoon of June 21. 1958 but there was no evidence to prove what had actually happened. It further held that the appellant had intended to take disciplinary action against the workman but subsequently departmental proceedings were dropped and action was taken under r, 18(b) of Standing Orders. The Tribunal also pointed out that no attempt was made before it to defend the action taken under rule 18 (a) by proving the alleged misconduct. Two witnesses were produced before the tribunal in connection with the alleged offence but the Tribunal did not rely on them on the ground that the important witnesses, namely, the Engineer, the Secretary and other members of the staff whose evidence would have been of more value had not been produced and no explanation had been given why they were not produced. The tribunal therefore held that on the facts it could not come to its conclusion that Sankaran had come drunk to the Mill and abused or attempted to assault either the Engineer or the Secretary or the other officers. In appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The Industrial Court has the right to inquire into the causes that might have led to termination of service even under a rule like 18(A). The employer could defend the actions under r . 18(c) by leading evidence before the Tribunal to show that there was in fact misconduct and therefore the action was bona fide and was not colourable exercise of the power under that rule. (ii) Even if the inquiry was not held by the appellant and action taken thereunder, it is now well settled that the employer could dismiss the action under r ' 18(d).

The appellants were the owners of a theatre. The receivers granted a lease of the theatre on certain terms and conditions to two persons, Raval and Faraqui. By an agreement dated November 27, 1954, between Raval and Garaquii on the one hand and Messrs. Filmistan Distributors (India) Private Ltd., hereinafter called "Filmistan" instituted suit No. 149 of 1960 in the Court of Small Causes Ahmedabad against Raval and two other persons claiming a declaration that it was entitled pursuant to the agreement dated December 1, 1960, to exhibit motion pictures in the theatre. By order dated December 31, 1960 the suit was disposed of as compromised. It was inter alia agreed that Raval and Earaqua were bound and liable to allow Filmistans to exercise their "exhibition rights" in the Theatre; that Raval, their servants and agents were not to have any right to exhibit any picture in contravention of the terms and condi tions of the agreement. The trial Judge passed an order disallowing the objection raised by the appellants. The revision application against that order was dismissed in limine by the High Court. When the case reached hearing and the evidence of a representative of Filmistna was being recorded, counsel for the defendants asked in cross examination the question whether the "agreement between the plaintiff and the defendant Nos. 5 and 6 were barred on principles of res judicata" from agitating the question that the said document dated November 1, 1954 as confirmed by their letter dated January 31, 1955 and further confirmed by document dated December l, 1960 was not a lease; and that in any event the suit No 149 of 1961 was for declaration of the rights of Films to exhibit cinematograph films, in view of section 92 of the Evidence Act. The High Court dismissed the revision application. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants (i) that an enquiry into the nature of the legal relationship arising out of the document could be permitted to 'be put to the witnesses for Filmisthan; and (ii) that the consent decree in suit No, 149 of 1953 had not decided that the agreement was of the nature Of a lease. HELD : (i). The order passed by the trial court is set aside and the Trial Court is directed to proceed and dispose of the suit. [446 E] (ii). A consent decree accord ing to the decisions of this Court, does not operate as res judicata, because a consent decree is merely the record of a contract between the parties to a suit, to which is superadded the seal of the court. A matter in contest in a suit may operate as Res judicata only if there is an adjudication by the Court : the terms of section II of the Code leave no scope for a contrary view. [441 G] (iii) The expression "case" is not limited in its import to the entirety of the matter in dispute in an action. This Court observed in Major section Khanna vs Brig. F. J. Dillon, [1893] 1 K.B.D. 426, that the expression " case" is a word of comprehensive import and includes a civil proceeding and is not restricted by anything contained in section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code to the extent to which the Court, viz., the trial Court in the instant case, proposed to go into that question and allow the whole question, that was closed once for all by consent decree of December 1.

The said term was extended retrospectively upto 20th of August, 1985 by an order passed in September, 1981 and it was again extended upto 31st March, 1983 by an Order dated 1st June, 1983. The appellant was acquitted by the Additional Sessions Judge, Chittoor of an offence under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life. The High Court reversed the finding of acquittal. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. An order of acquittal can be set aside for "substantial and compelling reasons" only and Courts used to launch on a search to discover those "substantial", and compelling reason". However, such expressions have been used more as flourishes of language, to emphasise the reluctance of the Appellate Court to interfere with an order of conviction than to curtail the power of the appellate court to review the entire evidence and to come to its own conclusion. [368C E] Sanwat Singh & Ors. vs State of U.P., A.I.R. 1971 S.C. 460, approved. Sanwat singh & Ors vs State Of Rajasthan, A.l. R. 1971 SC 460, referred to. In the instant case, the High Court was right in holding that the medical evidence supported the prosecution version and not the defence version. Merely because the Medical Officer stated that the victim could have received the injury if she was standing, it did not follow that the injury could have been received in the circumstances mentioned by the accused. The injury was inflicted with great force and its direction was upward. The location of the injury was 6 cms below the arm pit on the left side. According to the accused, the deceased received the injuries when she placed herself between P. W. 1 and himself. Therefore, it could not be said that an injury of the nature received by the deceased could have caused in the manner suggested by the prosecution that is, when the deceased was lying on her right side. It is obvious that he must have been upset by the persistent refusal of the brother and mother of the deceased to send her with him to his house. He probably attributed the refusal to reluctance on the part of his wife to accompany him straightaway. [369E F] Sanchal Singh & Anr.

The appellant was a Judge of the Supreme Court. He was convicted for having committed an offence under section 5(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The High Court dismissed his appeal and convicted him. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that (i) the President is given the power to appoint the Judges of the High Court as well as of the Chief Justice of the high Court by warrant under his hand and seal after consultation with the Chief justice of India, the Governor of the State and in a case of appointment of a Judge other than the Chief Jus tice, the Chief Judge of a High Court can be removed from his office by an order of the President passed after an address by each House of Parliament supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a minority of not less then two thirds of the members of that house present and voting, has been presented to the President in the same session for such removal on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity; (ii) the power under clause (c) is the President and it is in this manner that section 6(1) (c), which specifically enjoins that no court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 161(or section 165 of the Indian Penal Code, or under sub section (2) or sub section 3A) of section 5 of this Act, alleged to have been committed by a public servant, except with the previous sanction, (a) in the case of any other person, of the authority competent to remove him from his Office; and (b) in case of a person who is employed in connection with the affairs of the Union and is not removable from his offices save by or with the sanction of the Central Government. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power to punish a High court Judge, if one may so describe it, is to be found only in article 2 read with Article 124(4) and (5) of Article 124 of the Constitution. [835C] 2.1 In the case, the President has not been given the sole power or the exclusive power to remove a Judge either of the, Supreme Court or of theHigh Court from his place in order to enable that authority to grant sanction for prosecution of the Judge under the provisions of section 6 of the Act and this can be done only if it is read as a part of the scheme under which the public servant is required to furnish particulars of his assets with reference to which such an opinion can be formed and there is no vertical superior with legal authority enabling obtaining of information from the concerned Judge. [889E] 2:2 The President, therefore, being the authority Competent to appoint and to remove Judge, of course in accordance with the procedure envisaged in Article 124, clauses (4) & (5), placed before the President, a Judge by warrant, under his hands and seal, after consultationwith such of the Judges. [879E F] 2 :3 The power of appointment and removal of a judge other than those of the highest Court is not contemplated by section 6, but only for the purpose of deciding whether the offence under clause(e) of possession of disproportionate assets which the Public servant cannot satisfactorily account is made out prima facie. [869C] 4:1. The President has no power or authority to remove any Judge either from his residence or from his post except with a previous sanction.

The appellant was a member of a Scheduled Caste. Abhoy Pada Saha and Sudhir Kumar Mondal were the members of a scheduled caste. An election to a seat in the West Bengal Legislative Assembly from the Khargram Murshidabad constitutency reserved for members of the Scheduled Castes. The contestants at this election were Abhiman Pada, a member belonging to the Sunri caste which was a Scheduled caste. Sudhir objected to this nomination contending that Abhonoy Paada did not belong to any Scheduled Caste and that it was, therefore, not c open to him at the trial to contend, as he belonged to a smaller caste group of Sunirs known as Sahas. The Election Tribunal rejected this contention and dismissed the petition on the ground that he did not belongs to a Scheduled Castes specified in item 40 of the President 's Order. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) that the word "excluding" denoted that the Sahas contemplated would, but for this word have come within the Suniti caste, no question of Sahas being a distinct class independent of Sunriscould arise; and (ii) that in view of the fact that the Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950 was promulgated to indicate those castes who were to be considered as Scheduled Castes for the purpose of the Constitution. HELD: (1) The Tribunal came to its conclusion that it had not been prov ed in this case that the appellant belonged to any separate Saha caste or to any Saha Sunri sub caste of the Sunras caste. [390 C] (2) It was open to the respondent to show that the expression "excluding Sahas" meant excluding a smaller Caste group called Sahas, and it would have read "Sunri excluding those who bore the surname Saha. In the absence of such words "Saha ' must, in the context, be understood as referring to a larger caste group within the bigger caste group Of Sunris. [391 E F] (3) It is natural to think that when a statute says that a thing is to be excluded from another, both things are of the same kind; if one is a caste, the other must be a caste. It follows that when the item excluded Sahas from Sunris, since Sunri is a Caste group, Saha must equally be another caste group. [392 G] (4) The appellant was not a Sunri by caste and has not been proved to belong to the Scheduled Caste specified in Item 40 for greater safety o prevent them from claiming to be Sunris by reason of their origin.

The appellant was the tenant of a flat on the second floor of a building called "Ganga Vihar", Marine Drive, Bombay. The tenancy was a monthly one, the rent being Rs. 215. It is said that the appellant wanted to go to the United Kingdom for treatment of his failing eye sight and he got into touch with the police on 1 12 1948, and in conjunction with the latter, a trap was laid for the appellant. The complainant and the Sub Inspec tor were then taken to the appellant 's residence on 4 12 1948 and in connection with the raid held up the car of the appellant and recovered the sum of Rs. 30,500 from the rear seat of the car and also some papers, a typed draft of a partnership agreement was tween the complainant and his wife and the appellant, an application form for permission to occupy the building as caretaker. The appellant was charged under section 18(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, for receiving a pugree of Rs 29,500 and he was further charged under s 19(2) of that Act for receiving the said sum as a condition for the relin quishment of his tenancy. The defence of the appel lant was that he was in search of a partner to carry on his business during his intended absence, who was also to act as caRetaker of his flat anal that it was in this connection and with this object in view of his intended departure. The prosecution case was that the accused demanded a sum of RS. 30 lakhs which was later on reduced to Rs. 29, 500 as consideration for putting the complainant in vacant possession of the flat and an additional amount of Rs 2,000 for the furniture, and that the complainant agreed to pay these sums. The wife of the deceased denied any aiding and abetting. The Presidency Magistrate who tried the case convicted him under section 19(1)(c) of 'the Act and sentenced him to one month 's simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs 30,000. The appeal preferred by the appellant was summarily dismissed on 20 2 1950. On 10 4 1950 the wife of appel late was acquitted, the evidence being insufficient to prove any abetment. The High Court rejected this contention on behalf of the appellants based on the language of section 19 (1) and this is the only point which required our consideration. Held:(i) An assignment of the lease or transfer in any other manner by a tenant is not made an offence; the statute merely says that it is not a lawful transaction. It was the landlord 's consent to the transfer of a lease by sub lease or otherwise on receipt of consideration that has been made an offen cientence. The section in question, it should be further noted does not speak of relinquishment or giving up of possession,in general terms. (ii) In the case of an assignment, the assignor contin ues to be liable to the landlord for the performance of his obligations under the tenancy and this liability is contrac tual, while the assignee becomes liable by reason of privity of estate. The consent of the landlord to an assignment is not necessary in the absence of a contract or local usage to the contrary. But in the case Of relinquishment, it cannot be a unilateral transaction; it can only be in favour of the lessor by mutual agreement between them. (iii) In fact, a surrender or relinquishment terminates the lessee 's rights and lets in the lessor. It could only be made in favour o the lessor through mutual agreement. The relin cation of possession must be to the lessor or one who holds his interest.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was a partnership concern and the workmen of the Tata Engineering Company Ltd. were members of the T minority Employees Union. The company function as a consulting organisation and a service industry, and did not manufacture any product or carry on trade. Its work force consisted of engineers and supervisors and different categories of workmen. Out of 665 employees at Bombay, the draftsmen and the administrative staff number 306. These workmen were members Of the Tata Iron & Steel Company Ltd., and they served a Charter of Demands in July 1974 on the appellant and as their demands were not accepted and conciliation proceedings proved fruitless, the State Government made a reference of the dispute under section 10(1) (d), Industrial Tribunal, Maharashtra for adjudication. The Reference was numbered I. T. No. 292 of 1975. 170 The Union filed a statement before the Tribunal claiming an upward revision of the wage scales and dearness allowance and an increase from fifteen years to twenty years in the span for earning annual increments. It was urged that the Efficiency Bar as a feature of the wages scale should be removed, and that it would not be possible for the appellant to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the Union were accepted. The Tribunal rejected the demand of the union for dearness allowance on the basis of a slab system because that would have imposed an unacceptable burden on the company 's financial capacity and there was no reason why the existing scheme of dearness allowance should be disturbed when a substantial increase was being made in the level of the basic wage. On appeal, the Tribunal took note of the elaborate scales of wages already existing in the wage structure of the appellant, and decided to modify the existing structure of scales with flat increases in each category. But it rejected the claim of the company for dearness allowances on the ground that there would be a consequent increase in the dearness allowance or house rent allowance. The Industrial Tribunal also noted that after the salaries of the employees had been fixed in the respective scales, senior employees would have to be given some more increments in the new scales according to their completed years of service. Rs. 150/ per month and Rs. 100/ respectively and Rs., 100/ above the existing wage scales. The award was challenged by the workmen before the Industrial Tribunal which held that the existing wages were fair and reasonable on a region cum industry basis and that the increase envisaged there related to an increase in dearness allowance, it was not possible for it to bear additional financial liability if the demand demands of Union were accept. It also observed that in view of the increased burden of Rs. 50/ per mensem, the company should have fixed the dearness allowances in communion with the cost of living index and should not be a fixed amount. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the workmen that having regard to the financial capacity of the Company, the Industrial Tribunals erred in making the wage scale retrospective and, in any event, in ranging the retrospectivity back to 1st January 1976. It is urged that having due regard to its financial capacity, the appellant Tribunal erred in passing the wage rates retrospective and in any case, in increasing the retrospectivity, back to 21st January, 1976. On behalf of workmen it was submitted that the amendment results in the inclusion of a flat increase of Rs 150/ to each workman in the case of Draughtsmen and Rs 100/ and Rs, 100/ in the category of Draftsmen and of Rs,100/ to every employee in the other categories had been granted under the Industrial Disputes (Bombay) Rules, 1957. It would be noted that the Tribunal was betrayed by a curious confusion in accepting the plea of the Unions that a flat increased to the pay of each workman was intended in the original wage and, consequently, it fell into the error of amending the award.

The appellant, Sasamusa Sugar Works Ltd., and its workmen, the respondents an award had been made by an Industrial Tribunal fixing the pay of the employees at Rs. 2/2/ per day, and in pursuance thereof, the management of the appellant had entered into an agreement with the respondents that effect would be given to the wage structure prescribed by the said award. This agreement was subsequently published in Bihar Gazette as a part of the award. In spite of the Award and the agreement, the appellant paid its employees only As. / 10/ per month and that led to the present claim made by the respondents under section 15 of the Act. The respondents contended before the payment of wages authority that the refusal of the appel lant to pay to them wages at the rate awarded in substance amounted to an illegal deduction from their wages, and on that basis they asked for an order from the authority directing the appellant to pay the said prescribed wages. The appellant raised two pleas against the respondents ' claim. It was urged that section 15 Of the Act was inapplicable because the rates of wages fixed by the award did not fall within the definition of wages prescribed by section 2(vi) and it also argued, that the claim of the respondents was barred by limitation. The authority rejected the appellant 's contention and held that section 2 (vi) included wages prescribed under the Industrial Tribunal Act, and so it had rejected the appellants ' contention that the applications made by them were incompetent under section15 of the , and dismissed the petition. Held: (i) The basic assumption made by Mr. Setalvad in contending that section2(vi)(a) cannot take in the wages prescribed in the award is not well founded. When an award is made and it prescribes a new wage structure, in law the old contractual wage structure becomes inoperative and its place is taken by the wage structures prescribed by it. In a sense, the latter wage structure must be deemed to be a contract between the parties, because that, in substance, is the effect of industrial adjudication. The true legal position is that when industrial disputes are decided by industrial adjudication and awards are made, the said awards supplant contractual terms in respect of matters covered by them and are substituted for them. That being so, it is difficult to accede to the argument that the wages fixed under the award cannot be treated as wages under section 2.(vi) of the Industrial Disputes Act before it was amended. (ii) The amendment has merely clarified what, in our opinion, was included in the unamended definition itself. In this connection, the South Indian Bank Ltd. vs A. R. Chacko, A.I.R. 1964 S.C. 1523, and V. B Godse, Manager, Prabha Mills Ltd., vs R. M. Naick Inspector, under the Payment of Wages Act, the Bombay High Court has interpreted section 2 of the . (iii) to include wages directed to be paid by industrial adjudica tion.

The appellant was charged under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code for forging the thumb impression of Parma, and under section 477 A with having failed to enter them in the stock book. The trial Magistrate acquitted him but convicted him under section 465 and section 409 Of the Indian penal Code. On appeal by the State to the High Court it was discovered that there was no order sanctioning the prosecution and that sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure for his prosecution, that the evidence on record was insufficient to establish an offence either under section 466 or section 409, and that there having been an acquittal of the appellant by the trial Magistrate, the materials on record did not justify a reversal of that verdict by the appellate Court. Held, that sanction was required under section 198(1), as the official capacity was involved in the very act complained of as amounting to a crime; but if they do, then sanction is necessary. Shreekantiah Ramayya Munipalli vs The State of Bombay ([1948] L.R 75 I.A. 180) and Albert West Meads vs The King ([1947] L .R. 75 I A. 180), referred to. Held further that the acts with which the appellant was alleged could not be justified as done by virtue of his office, no sanction under s 197( 1) was necessary; and the absence of such sanc tion is fatal to the maintainability of the prosecution. Shree kantiah R. B. Gill vs The Queen ([1948) L. R 75 I .A. 185), distinguished.

The assessee was a public limited company incorporated in the State of Cochin with branches in that State as well as in what was British India and in Travancore State. It filed its income for the assessment year 1948 49, its accounting year being the previous calendar year. The Income tax Officer determined its assessable income to be Rs. 90 representing only the profit it made in Travancore state and under section 32(1) proviso (i) of the Travancore Act he refused a deduction of Rs. 79,275 shown as loss from branches situate outside the State. The assessee 's appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was unsuccessful but the Appellate Tribunal held that the banking business of the assessee being one and indivisible for the purpose of determining the amount assessable to income tax it was entitled to deduct the losses incurred outside Travancore State from the profits accruing and arising in that state. At the instance of the Commissioner of Income tax the following question was referred to the High Court of Travancore Cochin: " Whether on the facts and circumstances of the case the loss of Rs 27,709 arising in Cochin State could be set off against the profit of Rs." The assessee contended that the first proviso to section 24(1)(i) did not apply to the head business business but only introduced an addendum that where the profits of the business arose in what is British India in the case of Travancore Act and the losses under the head 'business were sustained in an Indian State or in the latter case in any other Indian State, these losses could not by virtue of the proviso be deducted from profits made in British India or Travancore State as the case may be. Held, that the object of section 24 was to allow a set off of profits arising under different heads and only in such cases could recourse be had to section 25(1). Arunachalam Chettiar vs Commissioner of Incometax, Madras ([1950] S.C.R. 271), Ram Narain Sons Ltd. vs Assistant Commissioner of Sales Tax (2) , distinguished.

The first respondent, Shaw Wallace & Co., was incorporated in January 1946 as a Private Limited Company to take over the business of the partnership firm of the Shaw Wallace and Co. which had been doing business in India for about 60 years. In July 1947 the Private Limited company was converted into a Public Limited Company. The Head Office of the Company was at Calcutta. It had Branches in Bombay, Delhi and Via Madras. The general practice of the company both at the Head office and the Branch Offices appeared to have been to retire its employees at the age of 55 but in some cases the Company in its discretion permitted an employee to continue beyond that age. In September 1959 an agreement was entered into between the Company and its employees for the retirement age of 58 subject to the employees passing a medical examination on reaching the age Of 55 subject to certain employees passing medical examination. The first respondent claimed that no workman should be retired from service before he bad completed 60 years of age. This dispute was ultimately referred to the Industrial Tribunal, Maharashtra. Before the Tribunal the Company resisted the workmen 's claim but submitted that it was agreeable to introduce for its Bombay employees provisions similar to those which had earlier been introduced by agreement for the Calcutta employees retirement at the time of their retirement at 55 subject only to the employee passing a Medical examination on attaining the ageof 55. The Tribunal directed that the age should be 58 but the Company may in its wisdom and with the express or implied consent of the employee concerned continue an employee after he attains that age, and it was also directed that in case any particular region employees have been successful in their claim for fixing the age at 60 this very success is bound to raise in others in the region similar expectations. The Company appealed to this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the trend in Bombay region had been to fix the retirement date of retirement at 60 years and that it would be impossible to say that the decision of this Court in Dunzlop Rubber Co. Ltd., vs Workmen, ; , relied on by the Tribunal was erroneous on the whole unsound. Held: (i) The age of retirement for workmen in all industries should be fixed at 60. The very few departures from this practice which the Tribunal has mentioned are, in our opinion, wholly insufficient to indicate any slowing down of this trend. What the Tribunal had failed to notice is that instances which may justify a revision of the judicial opinion expressed on an earlier occasion about a particular trend must be strong and unambiguous and they must speak for the period both before and more particularly after the previous finding had been recorded in the matter. (ii) The Tribunal has referred to these observations but has brushed them aside in a way for which we find no justification. (iii) The approach adopted by the Tribu nal was not very commendable, and that its present conclusion that what was said by itself on an Earlier occasion and was confirmed by this Court was in fact inaccurate. If this Court had erred in making those pronouncements it would he first to admit such mistakes and to correct the error. (iv) The contention of the workmen that the Tribunal 's finding that in all the awards in recent times in various concerns in Bombay Region the trend had been about fix the retire age at 55 or 58 is not challenged before this Court, was rightly rejected by the tribunal.

The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to five years ' rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 100/ . The High Court, on appeal by special leave, held that the presumption that they were dacoits ought not to have been drawn since the circumstances did not admit the drawing of such a presumption in the case, and therefore it was necessary always to start with the lesser presumption and draw the higher presumption only when there is some other evidence to show the complicity of the persons in the crime itself. In appeal by Special Leave, HELD : The law advocated by Mr. Chari is not correct. If there is other evidence, to connect an accused with the crime, it may be drawn. It is not necessary to state categorically in this case that the person with whom the goods were found were the dacoits themselves. This presumption has been drawn and in our opinion rightly in this ease. [723 A] In the present case, the goods stolen were a large quantity of cloth taken for sale to the market. These goods were not sold and were being taken back to the dealers by the cartmen.) A large number of persons said to be 20 in number pelted stones at the cart men and looted the property. Immediately afterwards a number of searches were made and the goods found with various persons who were prosecuted as offenders and they had been presumed to be involved in the dacoity itself. It may be 723 impossible to think that these 20 persons were merely receivers of stolen property from some other 20 persons who are the dacoits. The time gap in some cases is as short as two days and in some others it is not more than five days. In two cases only the time gap is about 19 days. Even then, the time lag is too short for original offenders to have disposed of the property to these appellants Or to have left the goods in their custody till such time as the original offenders could take them away.

The Orissa Superior Judicial Service (senior branch) is a combined cadre consisting of officers holding purely judicial posts as well as posts which are essentially administrative in character. It consists of eight district and sessions judges, two additional district and Sessions Judges, secretary to Government in law department, superintendent and legal remembrance and ex officio additional law secretary to the government in law Department, member administrative tribunal and the Registrar of the Orissa High Court, in all 15 in number. All these officers are the members of the service of the State and they were before 1962 presiding over district courts or courts subordinate to them and as such were under the control of the High Court. In view of article 229 of the Constitution, the power to appoint the Registrar is exclusively that of the Chief Justice. Neither the High Courts as such nor the Governor has any hand in his appointment. The power to transfer a district judge from one post to another whether as a Judge or to one of the posts in the secretariat was in his hands. It appears that for some time past there were differences between the High court and the Government about the posting of some judicial officers. The High Court was anxious that a judicial officer occupying one of these administrative posts enumerated above should not, in the interest of judicial work, continue in that post for an unduly long time. The Government by its letter of April 2, 1965 intimated that it had no objection to adhere to the principle of three years service in an appointment at a particular station against a special post. But when it came to the question of implementing that policy, the Government was reluctant. Every time the High ' Court requested the government to release the three officers mentioned above for being posted as district and Session judges or addl. district and session judges as the case may be, the government turned down those requests on one ground or the other.

Section 15(1)(a) of the Punjab Pre emption Act, 1913 as it originally stood underwent substantial changes in 1960 and as a result thereof, a host of writ petitions 122 were filed in this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution challenging the constitutional validity of section 15 on the ground that it infringed Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitu tion. The appellant contended that since the suit land belonged to more than one co sharer and had not been sold jointly by all the co sharers, he was entitled to claim the right of pre emption under clause 'fourthly ' of section fifteen(1) (b). A similar question came up before this Court in Balwant Ram vs B. Baijnath Singh, ; , wherein a two judge Bench negatived the contention that it cannot stand after the pronouncement of this Court on the expression 'other co sharors ' in section 15(i)(b) and is therefore entitled to exercise the right conferred on him by that provision. The question was whether the suit lands belonged to different persons or not. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The object of the Legislature was to confer the right to pre empt on specified family members of the vendor or vendors in the first three clauses of section15(1). Under the Punjab Act, 1905, the corresponding provision, section 12, con ferred a right of preemption, in the case of a sale of a share of such land or properly held jointly, firstly in the lineal discendents of the vendee in male line in order of succession; secondly, in persons not included under first or second above, in order to of succession and thirdly, in other co shar ers jointly or severally. It will be noticed that priority for the exercise of the right owes statutorily fixed and even in the cases of those falling within the same class, the exercise Of right was regulated by the use of the expression, 'in order of inheritance '. The 1905 Act was repealed and replaced by the 1913 Act. Accord ing to section 15 of this Act before its amendment in 1960, in case of sale of share out of joint land or property, the right was conferred firstly on the lineal descendents who held under tenancy of the vendors or vendors; secondly in the co divideders jointly and severally. [123D E] 1.2. The expression ' other co Tra sharers ' was used in the fourth clause of the said provision to ensure that no co shar er is left out or omitted and not to deny the right teen to kinstolk cosharers covered by the preceding clauses. If the preceding clause were not erased from the statute book as unconstitu tional the kinsfolk would have exercised the right in the order of preference, for which no justification was found. [124E F] 1:3.

On behalf of the workmen it was contended that as the benefits under sections 47 and 49 of the Act are already admissible to workmen in Baroda with effect from December 14, 1969, and they are quite adequate, the Tribunal committed an error of law in granting the additional benefits mentioned above. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The scheme of the benefits admissible under the Act cannot be said to cover the work men 's demand for sick leave to the extent allowed by the Tribu nal. [83B] 2.1 In providing for periodical payments to an insured worker in case of sickness (sickness benefit) or for medical treatment or attendance to him or the members of his family, the legislature did not intend to substitute any of these benefits for the workmen 's right to get leave on full pay on the ground of sickness. [86C] 2:2 In providing that a person qualified to claim sickness benefit shall not be entitled to it for the initial waiting period of two days except in tho case of continuous illness of the nature mentioned therein, "With regard to sick leave, the argument on behalf of appellant was that benefits were granted by the , but that is not a bar to the demand of the workman for sick Leave. The reason is that the first proviso to section 49 of ' the Employees State Insurance Act does not cover all contingencies of sickness and in any event the first three waiting days are not covered. In view of the provisions of the , no provision need be made about sickness leave at all. That this Act has been applied, to the company and that the workmen of tile Company get the benefit of sick leave. [87D E] 2 :3 The Tribunal was, therefore, justified in its view that the workman are entitled to 7 days ' sick leave with wages on full emoluments for a period of seven days when he is certified by a competent medical officer to be ill for that or a longer period. Sickness is a serious misfortune to a workman for it not only prevents him from earning his normal wages but is a drain on his meagre financial resources by way of additional expenditure on food, nursing and visits to the medical centre etc. It has not been disputed before us that the "region cure industry" basis is suitable in cases like the present for examining any controversy regarding the work man 's demands for additional benefits, but it has been argued by the learned counsel for the appel lants that the award of the benefit should not be admissible on the grounds that it had not been allowed by other companies in the region. [88E F] 3:4 The Tribunal has examined this aspect of the controversy also and given adequate reasons for allowing the benefit to the workman of 7 days sick leave in a year to its employ ees in Bangalore and it is permissible to accumulate it upto 12 days in addition to the current year 's leave, under a settlement dated July 17, 1969 which is being continued even after the coming into force of the . [88F G] 4:5 The benefit of sickness leave was therefore lost when the Act was made applicable to the region from December 15, 1969.

The appellant was detained under the order of detention passed by the Government of Bombay on the 8th June, 1955. The grounds of detention were vague and there was no application of mind by the detaining authority to the existence or otherwise of the legitimate objects of detention. Held, that the obligation to furnish particulars and duty to consider whether the disclosure of any facts involved therein is against public interest, are vested in the detaining Authority not in any other. It was therefore necessary for the detaining authorities to have an idea of the grounds of preventive detention as furnished. The requirement for such a communication would arise only if the detenue feeling the grounds to be vague, asks for particulars. An obligation to communicate the decision not to disclose facts considered prejudicial to public interest may well be implied in such a situation. But in the absence of any such request by the detenue, the non communication of the decision cannot be held to have hampered his constitutional right of representation and an obligation to supply particulars has been recognised in the case of the State of Bombay vs Atma Ram Sridhar Vaidya (A.I.R. , referred to. Held further that the requirement for making a representation under article 22(5) of the Constitution on behalf of the Portuguese Government by means of his affidavit filed in the High Court was without any basis, in view of the affidavit of the Chief Secretary. The order of the detention was mala fide and was passed for the ulterior purpose of preventing the appellant from acting in any manner prejudicial to the security of India and to the relations of India with Portugal.

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army and was attached to the Army Ordnance Corps Training Centre, Secundrabad. It was alleged that on April 4, 1958 he committed acts of gross misconduct. The allegations were as follows : "Knowing Kumari Prakash as the daughter of a brother Officer, Rao assisted her in going away from her parents protection and planning to run away with a sepoy. " He then took her in his scooter to the unit lines of 51 1 Gurkha Rifles where he arranged her meeting with a tea shop nearby where she received a present of sari and blouse from the sepoys in his presence. " The respondent was charged under section 120B, I.P.C., for having committed acts which were gross misconduct and as such dismissed from service. The Central Government found it to be unsatisfactory and on April 9, 1959 an order was passed removing the respondent from service by the appellant. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal from service on the ground that r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954, was ultra vires the . The High Court allowed the petition holding that r, 14 of Army Rules was ultra rites and that the action taken thereunder was without any authority. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the words "subject to the provisions of this Act" occurring in section 19 makes section 19 subject to section 45 and the Central Government had thus no power to remove a person from the service in derogation of the provisions Of section 45. HELD : The power under section 19 is an independent power. Although section 19 uses the words 'subject to . , it speaks of removal of a personfrom the service. Section 45 provides that on conviction by court martial an officer is liable to be cashiered or to suffer such less punishment as is in this Act mentioned. For removal from the serv ice under section19 of the read with r.14 of the . Rules, the Central government may remove a "person from the Service". Rule 14 is such a rule : it is not ultra vires. It is not correct to say that there should be rules and subject to the provision of the Act and such rules, the C. Government may dismiss or remove from the services any person subject to this Act.

The appellant was a Panchayat originally constituted under the C.P. & Berar Panchayat Act, 1946. On June 1, 1959, the Bombay Village Panchayats Act, 1958 (Bombay Act III of 1959) came into force in Vidharba region and by virtue of this Act the appellant was deemed to be a Panchayat under the Act. On July 14, 1961, resolution No. 2 was passed which provided that octroi duty would be imposed on the goods coming within its local limits, viz., on January 14, 1964, and February 19, 1963. The appellant 's appeal before the Standing Committee was rejected by the Samiti as per its resolution dated April 6, 1963, because the same was not filed within limitation as per the provisions of the Bombay village Panchayat Act and rule 5 of Taxes and Fees Rules 1960. On January 26, 1963 the company filed an appeal under section 124(5) before the Panchayat Samiti, Parseoni, which heard the appeal on two grounds namely, firstly that it was necessary for the Panchayat to have the octroi limits fixed with the approval of the Collector before levying octroi under r. 21; and secondly that the Company was not importing tea within the limits of the Panchayat for consumption use or sale. The Standing Committee allowed the appeal of the company on both grounds namely first that it is necessary for 15 years to have octroi limits prescribed with the approved by the Collector, before levying tax under r .21, and therefore the levy of octroi from April 1, 1963 was regularised and also that the tea was imported into the Panchayat limits for consumption, use or dispose of. The company thereupon filed an application under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court challenging the validity of the levy on the grounds: (1) that r. 5 of the Fees Rules was intraviress, (2) that the Standing committee had no jurisdiction to decide the appeal as it was barred by limitation because r. 4 did not require the Panchayat by which its approval to the limits and the rate at which it is to be levied and (3) that it did not fix the octroi limit in accordance with law. Held, that the essential condition precedent for the levy as provided in rr. 3 and 4 was that what the Panchayat does is to consider objections and suggestions and then finally make its choice as regards two things i.e., (1 ) the tax or fee imposed and the rates at which the same is to he levied. The word 'rate ' occurring in r. 3(b) of the Rules means the rate from which it was to be levy, (ii) the octroi will be levied from that date provided by rule and not from a date specified in the notice.

Section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968 confers an arbitrary and uncanalised power upon the Administrator with the result that the licensed dealer is at his mercy while seeking permission to carry on money lending or banking business on the security of any article, ornament or both in the same premises in which he carried on business as such dealer. The High Court struck down sec. 28 only on the ground that it suffers from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been provided by reference to which the power conferred on the Administrator to refuse permission or grant permission should be exercised and that the section confers an unguided, uncanalised and uncanalalised power without any criteria for guiding the discretion of the Administrator. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Union of India that sec.28 is part and parcel of the entire scheme of Gold Control as envisaged by the Act and the object of the enactment and the scheme affords sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The policy and the Scheme of the Act together with the necessity to ensure prevention of circumvention of the other provisions of the , afford more than sufficient guidance in the matters of exercising the power of discretion conferred on him under sec. In fact, sec. 5(1) requires that the Administrator should have regard to the policy and purposes of the .Act in making his orders. Moreover against his order under that Sec a revision lies to Central Government which implies that he will have to make judicious use of his power or discretion and any improper exercise is liable to be corrected by a higher authority. If that be so it cannot be said that unfettered or uncanalised or arbitrary power has been conferred upon the Administration under sec . Moreover, regard must be had to be the nature of the restrictions imposed by the section. [955C D] Harakchand Ratanchand Banthias vs Asst. Collector of Central Excise Poona, II Division while declaring unamended sec. 27(6) in several of its clauses referred to certain concepts which Administrator was required to take into account, and these concepts were regarded as indefinite, uncertain and vague.

The properties involved in the suit consist of agricultural lands situated in Eragudi village, Musiri Taluk, Tiruchirappalli district. According to the appellants, the said lands had been granted in Inam to the ancestor of one Ambalathadum Pachai Kandai Udayavaravar Temple by the Carnatic Rulers before the advent of British power in India. The original grant deeds were not available; but at the time of settlement of the Inams in sixties of the last century, Inam title deeds were issued in favour of the family of Pachathai Kandi Udayaravar Temple at Eravudi village. The appellants averred that the properties covered by the grant bad been granted to the original grantee burdened with the obligation of performing certain services in a Matam; and that the said properties had been alienated from time to time, and as a result of the first alienation, the appellants became entitled to them. The trial Judge examined the whole evidence and came to the conclusion that the grant of the Inam was a personal inam and that it was not a grant in favour Of the religious endowment within the meaning of the Act. On appeal by the respondents, the lower appellate Court reversed the finding of the lower Appellate Court that the existence of the temple had not been proved; but held that the appellants had proved their title to the suit properties. The High Court also took the view that the question as to whether on facts proved in this case an inference can be drawn that the previous manager or trustee had been removed from office by other persons who were acting as de facto managers of a temple de facto, has not been discussed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that article 134 B would not apply to the present case because the alienations evidenced by Exts. A 3, A 6 and A 12 show that the alienors purported to transfer the properties not as Poojaris or managers of any temple but in their individual character as owners of the said property. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The question whether a transfer effected by the manager of a Hindu religious endowment on the basis that it belongs to him and not to the religious endowments, is irrelevant for the purpose of article 134B if it is shown to have been made on the foundation that the transferor treated the properties as his own, it does appear that the two earlier Privy Council decisions in Gnanasambanda 's case lend some support to the contention. (2) The character of the representations made by the previous managers in regard to their relation with the property which is the subject matter of transfer, is relevant for the purposes of article134 B.

The appellant, a partnership firm consisting of himself and the two persons aforementioned, was carrying on business in the Apsara Theatre. The appellant, who had retired from the firm and was running a cinema theatre, applied to the District Magistrate under section 3 of the Jammu and Kashmir (Cinematograph) Act, 1989 for permission to construct a modern Cinema Hall at the proposed site, a detailed description of which was furnished in the plan annexed to the application. The District Magistrate rejected the said request by a detailed order dated April 21, 1979. On appeal, the District Judge held that the renewal of the licence could not be made in the name of any party other than the original licensee, namely, Shri Ved Gupta, who was declared to be the sole licensee in respect of the APSara Theatre and directed that the requisite licence for running the Cinema Theatre may be issued to him under the Act and Rules. On July 22, 1969, a notice to the appellant, proposing to commence an venture to construct and operate an air conditioned cinema in a plot of land which he proposed to take on lease in Gandhi Nagar, Jammu, in Collaboration with two osher persons, namely Todar Mal and Kishan Kumar in their own names shall not be their personal property but shall be their Personal property. The notice was served upon the appellant on July 22. 1969, by a letter dated September 24, 1980, requesting that the required licence for starting the Cinema theatre may be granted "in the name" of the "premises of Apsar Theatre situated at Gandhi Nagar Jammu". The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court and the same was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants (i) that the impugned order was violative of principles of natural justice inasmuch as the said procedure had not been followed by the District Collector, Jammu; (ii) that even though the licence had originally been issued in the names of Ved Gupta and six of the partners automatically acquired an interest in the licence, the other partners automatically acquire interest in it; (iii) that under the provisions of the statute prohibiting exhibition of cinematograph films in public by any one other than licensee or his authorised representative, the licensing authority was vested with exclusive jurisdiction to suspend a licence pending the proceed ings for such revocation and (iv) that since Ved Gupta had been expelled from the partnership and had thereby ceased to be connected with the firm, he did not have the possession of the premises and he was not entitled to claim a renewal of his licence. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The impugned order is one obviously passed by the district Magistrate in exercise of his function of administering the provisions and the Rules clearly include the power to take all incidental steps necessary for effective enforcement of the Statute. [595D] 1.2 In the instant case, the impugned orders are one purely passed by a District Magistrate in the exercise of its functions of administering cinematograph films and the powers to administer and enforce the provisions thereof and the implied power to control the exhibition of the cinematograph films is publicly exhibited by persons other than licensees.

The respondent entered into an agreement with the appellants, for a period of five years on the terms and conditions set out therein.
